g9-economics-ue3-t1.overview: Every economy begins with resources, the inputs used to produce goods and services. This lesson distinguishes free resources from scarce economic resources and matches the four factors of production with their factor payments.
objectives: Define resources and identify the two types of resources
Explain the test that separates free resources from economic resources
Describe the four broad categories of economic resources
Match each factor of production with its factor payment
Classify Ethiopian examples of resources into the correct category
g9-economics-ue3-t1.simple: Resources are the inputs used in production to make goods and services available to a society. There are two types: free resources and economic resources. A free resource is so abundant that people can have all they want at zero price, like air, sunshine and a mountain stream. An economic resource is scarce, so it has a price; price is the test of whether a resource is free or economic. Economic resources fall into four categories: land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship. Each factor earns a payment called a factor payment: labour earns wage, land earns rent, capital earns interest, and entrepreneurship earns profit.
g9-economics-ue3-t1.detailed:
What resources are. Resources are inputs used in the process of production in order to make goods and services available to the society. Without resources, no economy could produce the food, clothing, shelter and services its people want. Resources are divided into two broad types: free resources and economic resources.

Free resources. A resource is said to be free if the amount available to a society is greater than the amount people desire to have at zero price. Free resources are the free gifts of nature; they are unlimited in supply and have no prices. Examples include air, sunshine, solar energy and a mountain stream. Nobody has to produce more air, and nobody pays a price for breathing.

Economic (scarce) resources. A resource is said to be economic or scarce when the amount available to a society is less than what people want to have at zero price. Because they are not available in plenty, economic resources have non-zero prices. Price is the test of whether a resource is an economic good or a free good. Scarce resources include all types of human resources (manual, intellectual, skilled and specialized labour), most natural resources such as land (especially fertile land), minerals, clean water, forests and wild animals, all types of capital resources like machines, intermediate goods and infrastructure, and all types of entrepreneurial resources.

The four categories of economic resources. Economic resources can be divided into four broad categories: land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship. Labour refers to the physical as well as mental efforts of human beings in the production and distribution of goods and services; the reward for labour is wage. Land refers to all natural resources, or all the free gifts of nature, used in the production of goods and services; the reward for the services of land is rent. Capital refers to all the manufactured inputs that can be used to produce other goods and services, such as equipment, machinery, and transport and communication facilities; the reward for the services of capital is interest.

Entrepreneurship. Entrepreneurship is a special type of human talent that helps to organize and manage the other factors of production to produce goods and services. The entrepreneur takes the risk of making losses: if the business fails, it is the entrepreneur who bears the loss. The reward for entrepreneurship is profit.

Why the distinction matters. Only scarce resources force society to choose. Free gifts of nature satisfy whoever needs them without sacrifice, but economic resources must be allocated among competing uses, which is why their ownership earns them a price and a factor payment.

keyTerms.def: Inputs used in the process of production to make goods and services available to the society.
A resource available in greater amount than people desire at zero price; a free gift of nature with no price, like air and sunshine.
A scarce resource available in smaller amount than people want at zero price, so it has a non-zero price.
All natural resources, the free gifts of nature, used in production; its reward is rent.
The physical and mental efforts of human beings in the production and distribution of goods and services; its reward is wage.
All manufactured inputs used to produce other goods and services, such as machinery and transport facilities; its reward is interest.
The human talent that organizes and manages the other factors of production and takes the risk of losses; its reward is profit.
The reward earned by a factor of production: wage for labour, rent for land, interest for capital, profit for entrepreneurship.

workedExamples.problem: A farmer in Arsi uses his fertile plot, hires two daily labourers, rents a tractor and manages the whole wheat business himself. Identify each resource used and its factor payment.
workedExamples.given: Purchased inputs: fertile land, labour services of two daily labourers, tractor services, and the farmer's own organizing and risk-taking.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: land earns rent, labour earns wage, capital earns interest, entrepreneurship earns profit.
workedExamples.substitution: Fertile plot is land; daily labourers are labour; the tractor is capital; the farmer's organizing and risk-bearing is entrepreneurship.
workedExamples.calculation: Each resource is matched with its factor payment: the factor services are paid in the order land-rent, labour-wage, capital-interest, entrepreneur-profit.
workedExamples.answer: Land earns rent for the plot, labour earns wage, the tractor earns interest as capital, and the farmer as entrepreneur earns profit.

workedExamples.problem: Classify these items as free or economic resources: sunshine, clean water in a growing town, air, fertile farmland, minerals.
workedExamples.given: Five items with no prices attached at first sight.
workedExamples.formula: Test: is the amount available less than what people want at zero price?
workedExamples.substitution: Sunshine and air are available far beyond what people want at zero price; clean water, fertile land and minerals are limited relative to wants.
workedExamples.calculation: Items people would pay for fail the free-resource test and become economic resources.
workedExamples.answer: Sunshine and air are free resources; clean water, fertile land and minerals are economic resources.

workedExamples.problem: A shopkeeper in Bahir Dar borrows 20,000 birr from a microfinance institution at interest, buys a deep freezer, and runs the shop herself. State who receives which factor payment.
workedExamples.given: Lenders supply capital; the shopkeeper organizes, manages and risks losses; herself and possibly an assistant supply labour.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: each factor of production receives its own reward.
workedExamples.substitution: The borrowed money used to buy the freezer is capital; the shopkeeper's management and risk-taking is entrepreneurship; her selling work is labour.
workedExamples.calculation: Interest goes to the lender for capital, wages go to the worker for labour, and whatever remains after costs is the entrepreneur's profit or loss.
workedExamples.answer: Microfinance receives interest, any hired worker receives wages, and the shopkeeper earns profit (or bears the loss) as the entrepreneur.

workedExamples.problem: Grade 9 students listed the following resources: a mountain stream, skilled nurses, a road, and an engineer who founds a new factory. Place each in its resource category.
workedExamples.given: Four items to be classified among free resources, labour, capital and entrepreneurship.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: match each item by its nature (gift of nature, human effort, manufactured input, organizing talent).
workedExamples.substitution: A mountain stream is a free gift of nature; nurses supply skilled labour; the road is infrastructure, a capital resource; the engineer organizing the factory is entrepreneurship.
workedExamples.calculation: Each item is compared with the definitions of the categories and placed where it fits.
workedExamples.answer: Free resource: mountain stream; labour: skilled nurses; capital: the road; entrepreneurship: the engineer who founds the factory.

commonMistakes: Calling every natural thing a free resource; only items unlimited relative to wants, like air and sunshine, are free.
Thinking price has nothing to do with scarcity; price is the test of whether a resource is economic or free.
Confusing capital with land; machinery and infrastructure are capital, while natural gifts like fertile soil are land.
Listing interest as the reward for entrepreneurship; interest is the reward for capital, profit is the reward for the entrepreneur.
Folding entrepreneurship into ordinary labour; the entrepreneur organizes the other factors and takes the risk of losses.
Assuming the term 'land' in economics covers only soil instead of all natural resources.
Forgetting that economists count mental effort, like the work of teachers and doctors, as labour.
applications: Identifying in a family farm which factor earns rent, wages, interest or profit.
Understanding why a plot near Addis Ababa is expensive: fertile, well-located land is scarce.
Comparing a water kiosk charge with free sunshine to see the free versus economic resource test in daily life.
Recognizing that university and TVET training raises the quality of the labour factor a worker supplies.
Explaining why infrastructure such as roads and telecom lines counts as capital in Ethiopian production.
Watching how an entrepreneur in your community takes the risk of profit and loss when opening a shop.
g9-economics-ue3-t1.summary: Resources are production inputs and come in two types: free resources, unlimited at zero price like air and sunshine, and scarce economic resources, which carry a price. Economic resources fall into four categories: land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship. Each earns its factor payment: rent for land, wage for labour, interest for capital and profit for entrepreneurship.

g9-economics-ue3-t2.overview: The natural resources that feed production are renewing themselves or running out. This lesson classifies resources as renewable and non-renewable and presents the reduce, reuse and recycle principles for conserving them.
objectives: Define renewable resources and give their examples
Define non-renewable resources and give their examples
Explain the difference in renewal speed between soil and sunshine
Describe conservation and explain why even renewable resources can be depleted
Apply reduce, reuse and recycle to daily Ethiopian life
g9-economics-ue3-t2.simple: Production resources fall into two categories. Renewable resources have the potential to be replaced over time through natural processes: sunshine renews daily, but soil formation may take hundreds of years. Examples are solar energy, wind energy, soil, trees, grass, geothermal pressure and ground water. Non-renewable resources have a stock that is limited or fixed, found in the ground: natural gas, coal, steel, aluminum and oil. Recycling can replenish them, but the overall supply stays nearly constant. Conservation means not misusing, spoiling or wasting resources. We conserve by reducing, reusing and recycling, and by protecting resources from pollution, because our future depends on them.
g9-economics-ue3-t2.detailed:
Two broad categories. Many types of resources go into producing goods and services, and they have been broadly classified into two categories: renewable resources and non-renewable resources.

Renewable resources. Renewable resources are resources that have the potential to be replaced over time through natural processes. The renewal process may be relatively quick, as with sunshine, which comes on a daily basis. Or it may be very slow, as in the formation of soil, which may take hundreds of years. Examples of renewable resources are solar energy, wind energy, soil, trees, grass, geothermal pressure and ground water.

Non-renewable resources. Non-renewable resources are resources whose stock or reserve is limited or fixed, and which are found in the ground. The available supply may be replenished through recycling, but the overall supply remains relatively constant. Examples of non-renewable resources are natural gas, coal, steel, aluminum and oil.

Conservation. All natural resources should be used wisely, and we must conserve them. To conserve means not misusing, spoiling or wasting things. This is especially true for non-renewable resources, whose stock cannot grow. However, even some renewable resources can be depleted, that is run out, if they are all killed or overused. We must also protect natural resources from pollution, which occurs when people put harmful chemicals and other things into nature. Oil spilled into water, toxic chemicals in the air, and garbage dumped on the side of the road are examples of this problem.

Reduce. To conserve natural resources you can reduce, reuse and recycle them. Reduce by turning off the lights when you are not in a room, which cuts the fossil fuels used to generate electricity. Ride your bicycle and walk more to reduce the amount of gasoline used to transport you.

Reuse. You can reuse things like plastic jugs, jars, paper and bags. Each time you reuse something, you conserve the natural resources that would have been used to make a new one.

Recycle. Recycling means reusing a natural resource or product to make something new; it also means collecting and sending these things for reuse. Items that can easily be recycled include glass, some plastics, paper, cardboard, aluminum and steel. Some plastics and metals are hard to recycle because they are made from mixtures of materials, and mixtures can be hard to separate. So try to buy and use things that you can recycle. In general, both renewable and non-renewable natural resources are important to all of us, our future depends on them, and we must conserve and use them carefully.

keyTerms.def: A resource with the potential to be replaced over time through natural processes, such as solar energy, wind energy, soil and trees.
A resource whose stock or reserve is limited or fixed and which is found in the ground, such as coal, oil and natural gas.
The natural replacement of a resource over time, which can be quick, like daily sunshine, or very slow, like soil formation over hundreds of years.
Restored in supply, as when non-renewable resources are recovered through recycling, keeping the overall supply nearly constant.
Not misusing, spoiling or wasting natural resources; using them wisely.
Reusing a natural resource or product to make something new, including collecting and sending materials for reuse.
Putting harmful chemicals and other things into nature, such as oil spilled into water or toxic chemicals in the air.
Non-renewable fuels like coal, oil and natural gas used, for example, to generate electricity.

workedExamples.problem: A student lists these resources and asks which renew: the morning sun, coal under a mountain, grass regrown after grazing, and oil in a ground reservoir. Classify them.
workedExamples.given: Four items to be sorted by the renewal test.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: renewable resources can be replaced through natural processes; non-renewable stocks are limited or fixed.
workedExamples.substitution: Sunshine returns daily and grass regrows; coal and oil stocks are fixed in the ground.
workedExamples.calculation: Compare each item's renewal speed with the definitions: quick or slow natural renewal versus essentially fixed stock.
workedExamples.answer: Renewable: sunshine (quick) and grass. Non-renewable: coal and oil.

workedExamples.problem: In many Ethiopian homes, jugs and jars are re-served after their first use. Which conservation practice is this, and what does it achieve?
workedExamples.given: Used containers are kept in service instead of being thrown away.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: conservation uses the three actions reduce, reuse and recycle.
workedExamples.substitution: Re-serving jugs, jars, paper and bags is reuse, since nothing new is manufactured.
workedExamples.calculation: Each act of reuse conserves the natural resources that would have been used to make a new container.
workedExamples.answer: Reuse; each reuse saves the natural resources that making a new jug would have consumed.

workedExamples.problem: A pair of students compares two habits: leaving lights on in the empty classroom, and turning them off when leaving. Which habit conserves resources and why?
workedExamples.given: Electricity is largely generated from fossil fuels.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: reduce means cutting the amount of a resource used, so less fossil fuel is burned.
workedExamples.substitution: Lights left on waste electricity; turning them off reduces the generation demand.
workedExamples.calculation: Less electricity demanded means fewer fossil fuels used to generate it, so the second habit is the conserving one.
workedExamples.answer: Turning the lights off reduces the fossil fuels used to generate electricity.

workedExamples.problem: A collection drive sorts glass, combined-material plastic toys, cardboard and aluminum. Which items recycle easily, and which are hard to recycle?
workedExamples.given: Easily recycled items include glass, some plastics, paper, cardboard, aluminum and steel; mixtures are hard to separate.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: items made of mixtures of materials can be hard to separate, so they are hard to recycle.
workedExamples.substitution: Glass, cardboard and aluminum are single materials; the plastic toys combine materials.
workedExamples.calculation: Single-material items go straight into recycling; the mixed-material toys resist separation.
workedExamples.answer: Glass, cardboard and aluminum recycle easily; the mixed-material plastics are hard to recycle.

commonMistakes: Believing renewable resources can never run out; overused or killed resources, even renewable ones, can be depleted.
Thinking recycling raises the total stock of non-renewable resources; recycling only replenishes supply while the overall stock stays nearly constant.
Listing soil as non-renewable because soil formation is slow; slow renewal is still renewal, so soil is renewable.
Equating conservation only with recycling, ignoring reduce and reuse.
Thinking conservation is the government's job only, when everyday actions like turning off lights conserve resources.
Forgetting that pollution, such as oil spilled into water, damages natural resources as much as overuse does.
Buying mixed-material items without realizing mixtures are hard to separate for recycling.
applications: Switching off classroom lights to reduce the fossil fuel used to generate electricity.
Walking or cycling short distances to cut gasoline use and stay healthy.
Reusing jugs, jars, paper and bags instead of buying new ones.
Collecting glass, paper, cardboard and aluminum from campus for recycling.
Reporting or cleaning garbage dumped on the side of the road to cut pollution.
Planting and protecting trees so this renewable resource is not depleted faster than it renews.
g9-economics-ue3-t2.summary: Renewable resources have the potential to be replaced by natural processes, quickly like sunshine or slowly like soil, while non-renewable resources such as coal, oil and natural gas have fixed ground stocks that only recycling can partly replenish. Conservation means not misusing, spoiling or wasting resources. Everyone can conserve through reduce, reuse and recycle, while guarding resources against pollution.

g9-economics-ue3-t3.overview: Markets are the places where buyers and sellers exchange goods, services, labour and financial assets. This lesson defines a market and describes the goods and services market, the labour market and the financial market.
objectives: Define a market and describe its physical and digital forms
Identify buyers and sellers as the market parties
Describe the goods and services market and trace its money flow
Describe the labour market at the macro and micro levels
Describe the financial market and its role in capital formation
g9-economics-ue3-t3.simple: A market is an institution where two parties, usually buyers and sellers, meet to facilitate the exchange of goods and services. Markets may be physical, like a retail outlet where people meet face-to-face, or digital, like an online market. Three types matter most. The goods and services market is where households purchase consumable goods and businesses sell their products, including stores, the Internet and any other exchange place. The labour market is where employees provide labour services and employers provide jobs. The financial market is where securities, currencies, bonds and other financial assets are traded; it gives businesses capital formation and liquidity and is the basis of capitalist societies.
g9-economics-ue3-t3.detailed:
What a market is. A market is an institution where two parties can meet to facilitate the exchange of goods and services. The parties involved are usually buyers and sellers. The market may be physical, like a retail outlet, where people meet face-to-face, or digital, like an online market, where there is no direct physical contact between buyers and sellers. Although there are many types of markets, this unit focuses on three: the goods and services market, the labour market and the financial market.

Goods and services market. This is the market where households purchase consumable goods and services and businesses sell their goods and services. It includes stores, the Internet and any other place where consumer goods and services are exchanged. When you go to the store, shop on the internet, or even just trade with your friend, you are dealing in this market. It is here that end products are traded: consumers pay money to businesses to acquire something, so money flows from the consumer to the business firms continuously.

Labour market. The labour market is the market in which employees provide the labour services and employers provide the employment opportunities for labour. It should be viewed at both the macroeconomic and the microeconomic level. Daily labourers, domestic workers, skilled workers and professionals are examples of people providing labour services in this market.

Financial market. A financial market is any place where securities, currencies, bonds and other financial assets are traded between two parties. This market is the basis of capitalist societies, and it provides capital formation and liquidity for businesses. It can be physical or digital, and examples include bond, stock and share markets.

Markets around you. In a big Ethiopian town you pass through all three markets at once: the Merkato stall where a household buys a bag of rice is the goods and services market; the daily labourer waiting at the roadside site is the labour market; and commercial banks, currency exchange and share dealing belong to the financial market. Listing and classifying the markets in your own surroundings, as the textbook activity asks, is good training for seeing the economy as a system of interconnected markets.

keyTerms.def: An institution where two parties, usually buyers and sellers, meet to facilitate the exchange of goods and services.
A market like a retail outlet where buyers and sellers meet face-to-face.
An online market where exchange happens without direct physical contact between the parties.
The market where households purchase consumable goods and services and businesses sell their products; end products are traded here.
The market in which employees provide labour services and employers provide employment opportunities.
Any place where securities, currencies, bonds and other financial assets are traded between parties.
Financial assets such as bonds and stocks that are traded in financial markets.
The building up of capital for businesses, a key service the financial market provides along with liquidity.

workedExamples.problem: A farmer sells teff at the local market, his son is hired as a daily labourer at a construction site, and he saves his money in a commercial bank account. Which three markets appear in this story? Careful: place each event in its correct market.
workedExamples.given: Three events: selling teff, being hired, depositing savings.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: classify by what is traded: end products, labour services, or financial assets.
workedExamples.substitution: Selling teff exchanges a good; the hiring exchanges labour; the deposit is a financial-asset transaction with a bank.
workedExamples.calculation: Goods trading belongs to the goods and services market; hiring belongs to the labour market; banking belongs to the financial market.
workedExamples.answer: Selling teff - goods and services market; the son hired - labour market; the bank deposit - financial market.

workedExamples.problem: A consumer pays 300 birr for a blouse online from a boutique, without meeting the boutique owner. Is this a market? What kind, and in which category?
workedExamples.given: An exchange over the internet between a buyer and a seller of a consumable item.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: markets may be physical or digital, and the goods and services market includes the Internet.
workedExamples.substitution: The boutique sells and the household buys an end product online.
workedExamples.calculation: Digital form does not prevent a market; the item traded is a consumable good.
workedExamples.answer: Yes; it is a digital market, and it belongs to the goods and services market.

workedExamples.problem: Rank these job titles by the kind of labour service supplied: domestic worker, daily labourer, professional nurse, skilled mason. Are they all in the labour market?
workedExamples.given: Four occupations of people providing labour services.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: the labour market covers employees providing labour services and employers providing employment opportunities.
workedExamples.substitution: All four groups supply labour services, from unskilled daily work to professional service.
workedExamples.calculation: The categories in the textbook for this market include daily labourers, domestic workers, skilled workers and professionals.
workedExamples.answer: Yes, all of them belong to the labour market; only the type of labour service differs.

workedExamples.problem: A firm wants to expand its factory and needs money, while a household has savings. Which market connects them, and what does the firm gain?
workedExamples.given: Households have savings; firms seek funds for investment.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: the financial market provides capital formation and liquidity for businesses.
workedExamples.substitution: Savings and securities are traded in this market between two parties.
workedExamples.calculation: The market routes the household's funds to the firm, giving the firm capital formation and liquidity.
workedExamples.answer: The financial market connects them; the firm gains capital formation and liquidity for expansion.

commonMistakes: Thinking a market must be a physical place where people meet; markets can be digital, like online trade.
Limiting markets to goods only, forgetting labour and financial markets.
Confusing the goods and services market with the labour market: goods are bought here, but labour is hired in the labour market.
Believing financial markets trade only shares; they trade securities, currencies, bonds and other financial assets.
Thinking the labour market is only a microeconomic topic, when it should be viewed at the macroeconomic level too.
Forgetting that money flows continuously from consumers to business firms in the goods and services market.
Assuming a trader with a friend has nothing to do with markets; even trading with a friend happens in the goods and services market.
applications: Recognizing Merkato stalls, supermarket aisles and online shopping as one and the same kind of market.
Classifying the hiring of seasonal workers on a coffee farm as part of the labour market.
Using a bank account or currency exchange and knowing this is the financial market at work.
Observing how money paid at a store shop flows continuously from the household to the business.
Listing the nearby markets in your surroundings and labelling each as goods, labour or financial.
Understanding why firms need the financial market to get the capital that funds investment and expansion.
g9-economics-ue3-t3.summary: A market is an institution where two parties meet to exchange goods and services, physically or digitally. The goods and services market is where households buy end products from businesses, sending money repay continuously in that direction. The labour market matches employees and employers, and the financial market trades securities, currencies and bonds, providing capital formation and liquidity for businesses.

a place where prices are fixed by law

questions.explanation: Securities, currencies, bonds and other financial assets are traded there.

questions.explanation: The textbook says the labour market should be viewed at both levels.

questions.q: Shopping on the internet places you in which market?

g9-economics-ue3-t4.overview: Income flows round and round an economy among households, firms and the government. This lesson introduces the circular flow of income, the real and money flows, and the two-sector and three-sector models.
objectives: Define the circular flow of economic activities and of income
Distinguish real flows from money flows
State the assumptions of the two-sector model
Explain the roles of saving, taxes, subsidies and transfer payments in the three-sector model
Construct and interpret a circular flow diagram
g9-economics-ue3-t4.simple: The circular flow of economic activities is a simplified macroeconomic model showing how households, businesses and the government interact in markets by exchanging goods and services, productive resources and money. Production, exchange and consumption are the three important economic activities, and the transactions they create move income and expenditure in a circle. Two kinds of flows appear: real flows, the factor services and goods that actually move, and money flows, the payments matched to them; the two are sides of the same coin. For closed economies there are two models: a two-sector model of households and firms, and a three-sector model that adds the government, which taxes, spends, gives subsidies and transfer payments.
g9-economics-ue3-t4.detailed:
What the circular flow is. The circular flow of economic activities is a simplified macroeconomic model of the basic economic relationships in a market economy. It gives an overview of how households, businesses and the government interact in different markets by exchanging goods and services, productive resources (inputs or the factors of production) and money. A circular flow of income is a visual model of an economy that shows how a currency, such as the Birr, flows through markets among decision-making units. These sectors are sometimes known as decision-making units of the economy, and are generally called economic agents.

How the flow arises. Production, exchange and consumption are three important activities of an economy. As people carry them out, transactions occur among the different sectors, and income and expenditure move in a circular way. A circular flow is a pictorial representation of the continuous flow of payments and receipts for goods and services and factor services among the sectors of the economy.

Two types of flows. Economic transactions generate two types of flows: real flows and money flows. Real flows consist of factor services flowing from the owners of factor services to the producers, and goods and services flowing from the producers to the buyers. Money flows consist of the money incomes paid for factor services, such as rent and wages and interest, and the money expenditures incurred for the purchase of goods and services. Real flows and money flows are two sides of the same coin: a real flow of goods and services is matched by an equal but opposite money flow.

The two-sector model. The two-sector model represents a private, closed economy with only the household sector and the business sector. Its assumptions: there are only two sectors; households are owners of the factors of production and supply factor services to firms; firms produce goods and services and sell their entire output to households; households receive income for their factor services and spend the entire amount on consumption; there is no saving; there is no government; and the economy is closed, with no exports or imports. In the diagram, the inner circle shows the real flow of factor services and goods and services, while the outer circle shows the money flow: firms pay households for factor services, households spend this income on goods from firms. So total money receipts of the firms equal the total income of the households.

The three-sector model. Here the economy has three sectors: households, firms and government. Government activity is divided into government revenue and government expenditure. Government gets its revenue by imposing taxes on households and on firms. It pays this revenue back by purchasing goods and services from them, by giving subsidies to firms, and by giving transfer payments to households. Households' savings are deposited in the capital market, which in turn gives the savings to firms for investment. In this way national income flows in a circular form among the three sectors.

A visual model that shows how a currency, such as the Birr, flows through markets among decision-making units.
The decision-making units of the economy, such as households, business firms and the government.
Flows of factor services from owners to producers and of goods and services from producers to buyers.
Flows of money incomes such as rent, wages and interest, and of money expenditures for goods and services.

A circular flow model whose sectors are households, firms and the government, adding taxes, spending, saving and investment.

workedExamples.problem: In a two-sector economy, trace what happens when a household supplies one hour of labour to a garment factory. Identify both flows.
workedExamples.given: The household supplies a factor service; the factory produces a good that the household buys with its income.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: real flows of factor services and goods are matched by equal but opposite money flows.
workedExamples.substitution: Real flow 1: labour service from household to firm. Money flow 1: wage from firm to household. Real flow 2: garment from firm to household. Money flow 2: expenditure from household to firm.
workedExamples.calculation: Every real move is paired with a money move in the opposite direction, so the two circles of the diagram stay balanced.
workedExamples.answer: Labour and the garment are the real flows; the wage and the purchase payment are the matching money flows.

workedExamples.problem: Under the two-sector assumptions, what happens to the economy in this case: a household saves half its income instead of spending it all?
workedExamples.given: The model assumes households spend their entire income on consumption and that there is no saving.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: the two-sector model requires total household income to be converted fully into consumption spending.
workedExamples.substitution: Saving half the income breaks the assumption that spending equals income.
workedExamples.calculation: If spending falls short of income, the money receipts of firms no longer equal household income, so the simple model no longer holds.
workedExamples.answer: The model's assumption is violated; the two-sector model only works with no saving.

workedExamples.problem: A government collects 100 million birr in taxes, pays 40 million for goods, 30 million as subsidies to firms and 30 million to needy households. Classify each outflow.
workedExamples.given: Revenue of 100 million birr from taxes on households and firms.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: government expenditure includes purchases of goods and services, subsidies to firms, and transfer payments to households.
workedExamples.substitution: The 40 million for goods is a purchase; the 30 million to firms are subsidies; the 30 million to households are transfer payments.
workedExamples.calculation: All three are government expenditure that injects tax revenue back into the circular flow.
workedExamples.answer: Purchases: 40 million; subsidies to firms: 30 million; transfer payments to households: 30 million.

workedExamples.problem: In the three-sector model, what role does the capital market play between households and firms?
workedExamples.given: Households save part of their income; firms need funds for investment.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: savings are deposited in the capital market, which gives savings to firms for investment.
workedExamples.substitution: Household savings flow to the capital market; the capital market passes funds to firms.
workedExamples.calculation: The linkage converts saving leakage back into investment injection, keeping the circular flow going.
workedExamples.answer: It collects household savings and channels them to firms for investment.

commonMistakes: Thinking circular flow describes only goods, forgetting factors, money and government.
Reversing the direction of flows: money flows opposite to real flows in each exchange.
Assuming the two-sector model includes the government, banks or foreign trade; it excludes all of them.
Forgetting the two-sector assumption of no saving and no exports or imports.
Saying real flows and money flows are independent; they are two sides of the same coin, each matched by an opposite flow.
Believing the government only taxes; it also purchases goods, subsidizes firms and makes transfer payments.
Ignoring the capital market that links household savings with firms' investment in the three-sector model.
applications: Tracing your own family's circular flow: factors supplied at work, wage received, purchases made, taxes paid.
Seeing how a government school teacher's salary ties the household sector to public spending.
Understanding why a bank deposit in an Ethiopian bank helps fund firms' investment.
Interpreting how a new government subsidy affects the flow between the state and firms.
Using the real and money flow distinction to explain why GDP can be measured by either income or spending.
Drawing the two-sector diagram to show why firms' total receipts equal households' total income.
g9-economics-ue3-t4.summary: The circular flow of income is a visual model of how money and resources move continuously among decision-making units such as households and firms. It contains real flows of factor services and goods matched by opposite money flows of wages, rent and expenditure. The two-sector model of households and firms assumes no saving, no government and a closed economy, while the three-sector model adds the government with taxes, purchases, subsidies and transfer payments, and connects saving to investment through the capital market.

g9-economics-ue3-t5.overview: Land is the backbone resource of an agricultural country like Ethiopia. This lesson examines Ethiopia's land area, its two main highland soil types, the climatic advantage of agro-ecological zones, and the history and limits of state land ownership.
objectives: Explain why land is a vital economic resource in Ethiopia
State Ethiopia's total area and the share considered suitable for agriculture
Identify the two main soil types found in most Ethiopian highlands
Explain how agro-ecological zones raise the land's resource potential
Describe the evolution of land ownership from 1975 to the present state ownership
g9-economics-ue3-t5.simple: For Ethiopia, where agriculture is the backbone of the economy, land is a very important economic resource. In agriculture, land means both areal extent and the productivity of crops. Ethiopia covers a total area of 1,106,000 square kilometers, of which 35 percent is considered suitable for agriculture (CSA, 2007), thanks to good soil and suitable climate. Most of the highlands have two main soil types: red-to-reddish brown soils, rich in minerals, well drained and easy to plough; and brownish-to-grey and black soils with high clay content, which have excellent potentials with proper drainage and conditioning. Altitude creates different agro-ecological zones that multiply the land's potential and support exportable crops that earn foreign currency. Land was held unequally under the feudal system until 1975, and since then the state has owned land, though rural people hold lifetime rights and urban residents lease land for 99 years.
g9-economics-ue3-t5.detailed:
Why land matters in Ethiopia. For a country like Ethiopia, where agriculture is the backbone of the economy, land is a very important economic resource. In the context of agriculture, land refers to areal extent as well as its productivity of food crops and other crops. Ethiopia has a total area of 1,106,000 square kilometers, of which 35 per cent is considered to be suitable for agriculture (CSA, 2007). The availability of this amount of land for agriculture is directly or indirectly the result of good soil and a suitable climate.

The two main highland soils. Most of the Ethiopian highlands have two main soil types that are generally believed to be suitable for agriculture. Red-to-reddish brown soils are well endowed with the required minerals for crops and are found in areas of relatively good drainage; they are friable, meaning easy to plough. Brownish-to-grey and black soils with high clay content have excellent agricultural potentials when they receive proper drainage and conditioning.

The climatic bonus. The formation of different agro-ecological zones due to altitude has multiplied the resource potential of the land of Ethiopia. The presence of different agro-climate zones allows the growth of different types of crops, which increases Ethiopia's potential to produce exportable items and earn foreign currency.

From feudal land to state land. The Ethiopian people struggled for centuries against inequitable land holdings and effectively removed the feudal system in 1975. The socialist system that came into being in 1975 under the slogan 'Land to the Tiller' paradoxically overturned that slogan and ended up in state ownership rather than giving land to the people. The government that took power in 1991 was expected to solve land rights problems by giving land to the people in tenure, but it maintained state ownership and controls all urban and rural land together with natural resources.

Rights under state ownership. Although the state owns the land, rural peasants and pastoralists are guaranteed a lifetime 'holding' right that gives all rights except sale and mortgage. Even if it is not mentioned in the constitution, urban residents are also provided the right to get land for residence on a 99-years-lease basis agreement. State ownership is far from ideal, however, because it restricts the different land rights of use, rent, lease, endowment and inheritance. Since redistribution of land is highly restricted, access to rural land is also almost non-existent.

Compensation and the way forward. The constitution is commended for protecting land holdings against arbitrary state eviction by providing for a 'commensurate' amount of compensation during expropriation. However, successive implementation of proclamations has violated this protection by denying market value, that is fair compensation, for loss of property; the amount of compensation in the event of expropriation is insufficient. By creating more access to rural land, liberating land holding rights, and compensating fairly for lost property during expropriation, the government could give more secure land rights than its predecessors.

keyTerms.def: In the context of agriculture, the areal extent of a country and the productivity of its food crops and other crops.
Highland soils well endowed with the minerals required by crops, found in areas of good drainage and friable, that is easy to plough.
High-clay-content highland soils that have excellent agricultural potentials with proper drainage and conditioning.
Easily worked or ploughed, a quality of the red-to-reddish brown soils.
Farming zones created by differences in altitude, allowing many crop types and multiplying Ethiopia's land potential.
The lifetime right of rural peasants and pastoralists that grants all rights over land except sale and mortgage.
The 99-years-based agreement through which urban residents obtain land for residence.
The state's taking of property, for which the constitution promises a commensurate amount of compensation.

workedExamples.problem: Ethiopia's total area is 1,106,000 square kilometers and 35 per cent of it is suitable for agriculture (CSA, 2007). About how many square kilometers is that?
workedExamples.given: Total area: 1,106,000 sq km; suitable share: 35 per cent.
workedExamples.formula: Suitable area = Total area x suitable share
workedExamples.calculation: 1,106,000 x 0.35 = 387,100 square kilometers, roughly 387 thousand.
workedExamples.answer: About 387,100 square kilometers, roughly one third of Ethiopia's area, is suitable for agriculture.

workedExamples.problem: A highland farmer obtains a red-to-reddish brown soil plot, while his relative gets a black clay-rich plot on a sloping field. Using the textbook, advise each farmer.
workedExamples.given: Two plots: mineral-rich well-drained red soil; high-clay black soil without drainage works yet.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: red-to-reddish brown soils are mineral-rich, well drained and friable; black clay soils excel with drainage and conditioning.
workedExamples.substitution: The first farmer can plough directly since the soil is friable; the second must invest in drainage and conditioning first.
workedExamples.calculation: Compare each soil with the requirements named in the textbook for good crop performance.
workedExamples.answer: The red soil farmer can plough at once; the black clay farmer needs proper drainage and conditioning to unlock the soil's excellent potential.

workedExamples.problem: A rural widow holds land and passes it to her children, but she is told she cannot sell it or borrow against it. Does the holding right cover her actions?
workedExamples.given: The lifetime holding right gives all rights except sale and mortgage.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: holding right grants all land rights except sale and mortgage.
workedExamples.substitution: Passing land to children is use and inheritance, rights she holds; selling and mortgaging are excluded rights.
workedExamples.calculation: Compare each action with the granted and excluded rights.
workedExamples.answer: Yes, the passing to children is covered; but selling or mortgaging the land is not permitted under the holding right.

workedExamples.problem: A city plots a road through houses and offers payment far below market value. What does the constitution promise, and what practice violated it?
workedExamples.given: The constitution provides a commensurate amount of compensation during expropriation.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: expropriation should bring commensurate, that is fair market value, compensation.
workedExamples.substitution: The offer denies market value for the loss of property.
workedExamples.calculation: Compare the offer with the constitutional promise of commensurate compensation; the practice fails that test.
workedExamples.answer: The constitution promises commensurate compensation, but successive proclamation implementations denied fair market value, making the compensation insufficient.

commonMistakes: Thinking land in economics means only soil size, forgetting the productivity aspect in agriculture.
Reversing the soils: it is the red-to-reddish brown soils that are friable and well drained, while black clay soils need drainage and conditioning.
Believing the 1975 slogan 'Land to the Tiller' ended in private ownership; paradoxically it ended in state ownership.
Assuming land was privatized in 1991; the government maintained state ownership of urban and rural land.
Thinking holding right includes the right to sell or mortgage the land; those rights are excluded.
Forgetting that urban residents get residence land under a 99-years-lease basis, though it is not mentioned in the constitution.
Believing constitutional compensation is always honoured; successive proclamations denied market value compensation.
applications: Recalling that agriculture is the backbone of Ethiopia's economy when explaining land's importance.
Measuring that about 35 percent of Ethiopia's 1,106,000 square kilometers supports farming.
Choosing crops that fit the agro-ecological zone created by altitude in your own district.
Understanding why coffee, teff and other exportable crops grown in different zones earn foreign currency.
Tracking how holding rights affect a rural family's ability to keep, inherit and invest in land.
Following the debate over fair compensation when the state expropriates land for roads or industrial parks.
g9-economics-ue3-t5.summary: Land is vital for Ethiopia, where agriculture is the backbone of the economy: of the country's 1,106,000 square kilometers, 35 percent is suitable for agriculture (CSA, 2007) because of good soil and suitable climate. Most highlands hold friable, mineral-rich red-to-reddish brown soils and high-clay brownish-to-grey and black soils that excel with drainage and conditioning, while altitude-created agro-ecological zones multiplied crop diversity and export potential. Since 1975 the state owns all land; holding rights grant lifetime use except sale and mortgage, urban land runs on a 99-year lease, and compensation for expropriation remains unfairly low.
